beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: This is $100. Now picture $1 billion: one warehouse room packed with 10M of these notes. Sounds huge? That room is the smallest way to see a billion.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That was the short version. Here is what it left out: six more ways to feel how big a billion really is.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Spending it, earning it, saving it, the money it pays all by itself, how many people own one, and a last one that makes a billion look small.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Hold on. A billion is just a really big million, isn't it? How different can the two of them be?

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Ask anyone who has counted both. A million is a number you can picture in your head. A billion is a number nobody can.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way one. Spend it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Say you spend $1,000 every single day: rent, dinners, trips, anything you like, with nothing coming back in.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That comes to $365,000 a year, gone at the same steady pace, day after day.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: At that pace, how long would a whole million last me?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A million runs out in about 3 years. Long enough to feel rich, and short enough to end.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Now do the very same thing with a billion: the same daily spending, the same lifestyle, the same steady pace.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A billion lasts 2,740 years. If you had started back in ancient times, you would still be spending it today.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Same habit, wildly different endings: the million is gone in 3 years, while the billion runs for 2,740.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: The words play a trick on you. Million and billion sound like neighbours, but they live ages apart.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Fine, nobody just spends. So how long would it take to earn a billion with a paycheck?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way two. Earn it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan earns $50,000 a year at his office job, a solid salary that pays the rent and then some.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: And if I saved every cent of it, how many years until I hit a billion?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: No rent, no food, no tax: $1.00B divided by $50,000 a year comes to 20,000 years.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A million would take him 20 years. A billion takes 20,000, longer than recorded history.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A whole career of 40 years pays him $2.0M. A billion is 500 of those entire working lives.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: So nobody earns a billion with a paycheck. A salary, even a great one, is simply the wrong kind of money for it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Income and wealth are different animals: income is what you are paid for your time, and wealth is what you own.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So if a paycheck can never get there, what about saving and investing it for decades?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way three. Save it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan puts $500 a month into investments for 40 years, growing at an assumed 7% a year.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: That sounds like a really solid plan. So where does it actually get me?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: It grows to $1.3 million, and most of that is growth, because he only ever put in $240,000 himself.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: On paper, that makes Rohan a millionaire. Now set his whole pot down right next to a billion.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A billion is still $998.7M more than everything his plan grows to in 40 years.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: In our room of notes, his whole life of saving is one small bundle on the floor, and the rest of the room is still empty.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: I have known plenty of careful savers in my life. I never met one who saved a billion.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Spending, earning, saving: none of them come close. So how does the money keep coming for the people who already have it?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way four. It pays itself.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: If nobody earns it or saves it, then how do the rich keep getting richer every year?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Here comes the twist. A billion never has to be spent. At an assumed 4% a year, it pays $40 million every year, and the pile stays the same size.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rent from buildings, dividends from company shares, interest on bonds: things you own pay their owners.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Take just 4% of the pile out each year, and everything else stays exactly where it is.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That yearly income alone beats Rohan's entire career of pay by $38.0M, every single year, without lifting a finger.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: To earn what that billion pays in a single year, Rohan would have to work for 800 years.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: No salary ever teaches you this part. Once the pile is big enough, the pile does all the work.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Its name is passive income: money that comes from what you own, not from the hours you work.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: And it works at every size. A small pile pays a small amount, but it still pays while you sleep.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A billion keeps itself going, then. But how many people in the world actually have one?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way five. Count them.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Billionaires feel incredibly rare. So how many of them are there, really?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Forbes counted 3,428 billionaires in March this year, a record, and 989 of them live in the United States.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Together they own $20.1T. Split evenly, that is about $5.86B each.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So the average billionaire holds about 5.9× our whole room of notes, not just the one.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And the whole club is small enough to fit inside one sports arena, with plenty of seats left over.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: At Rohan's salary, all their money together would take 402M years of work to earn.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: And very little of it is cash, mind you. It is mostly shares in companies they built, and those prices move every day.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Five ways in, a billion is starting to make sense. Now meet the one fortune that makes a billion look tiny.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way six. Meet the richest.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So who sits right at the very top of that list?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Elon Musk, who runs Tesla and SpaceX. Forbes put him at $839B in March this year, the highest it has ever recorded.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: At Rohan's salary, earning that fortune would take 16.8M years of work, every cent saved.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And spending $1,000 a day, Musk would need 2.3M years to run out.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And almost all of it is shares, so it rises and falls with the stock price, sometimes by billions in a single day.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Now picture the richest fortune. Elon Musk's $839B is 839 of our rooms of notes: row after row of rooms, every single one of them packed full.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So a billion outlasts any spending, outruns any paycheck and dwarfs a whole lifetime of saving.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: What builds one is owning things that pay. So how many years would your own pay need?
